lesson:
In this lesson, we explore systems thinking and how it applies to AI challenges. Problem scoping is the most important and most difficult part of an AI project cycle, and systems thinking is a tool to help us understand and conceptualize these challenges. A system is defined as looking at the whole or the big picture, examining individual components and how they relate to each other through relationships. 

To understand systems, it helps to distinguish between complicated and complex scenarios. Complicated things have a lot of detail, but at the foundational level, they can be decomposed into mechanical and predictable operations, such as a mechanical watch. In contrast, a complex situation features interactions with so many potential consequences that it is not realistic to decompose it into elemental parts and predict the whole. Relationships add a dimension that requires viewing the system through a different lens.

We can look at real-world examples to understand systems, such as a predator-prey ecosystem simulator with foxes and rabbits. In this model, the foxes and rabbits are elements, and their relationships are represented by arrowhead lines. The rules of the simulator state that foxes eat rabbits if they are close, and they reproduce when they eat. If foxes go without eating for a certain period, they die and vanish. Meanwhile, rabbits bounce around, move, and spontaneously reproduce through duplication with some random chance. The dynamics of this model lead to an unpredictable outcome where increasing rabbits leads to increasing foxes, increasing foxes leads to decreasing rabbits, and decreasing foxes leads to decreasing rabbits.

To review, a system is made up of interconnected components called elements. Individual elements do not demonstrate the whole until they are put together, and the relationships between them make it a system. Systems thinking is understanding the elements and their interactions. When relating this to AI, we know AI has advantages over traditional solutions, and thinking about how AI enters a system helps us understand the consequences, relationships, and potential impacts on the ecosystem. 

When talking about AI and systems thinking, several prompts should be kept in mind: what are the relationships between elements, how does one impact another, how do individual actions impact the system as a whole, and could we introduce instability into our system? A real-world use case for systems thinking is the market for French fries. To anticipate what will happen with French fries, we examine the component elements: potatoes as the food source, oil for frying, water for growing potatoes, factories or tools for processing potatoes into french fry shapes, and salt or other seasoning for flavoring. 

Zooming in on potatoes, the supply is completely dependent on farming growth crops and output. Potatoes need sunlight, sunshine, healthy soil, and water, and crop damage creates a ripple effect. Drought and water issues lead to fewer available potatoes and rising costs. In the background of our minds, we consider where AI can play a role to help in this system. 

Regarding terminology and jargon, the factors in a system are called elements, connections are called arrowhead lines, and loops in the direction indicate feedback relationships. Graphical views show two types of relationships. A positive relationship means an increase in x leads to an increase in y. A negative relationship means an increase in x causes a decrease in y, as seen with foxes and rabbits. 

A potato system diagram places the potato at the center, impacted by crop damage, the cost of potatoes, and the weather. The availability of potatoes then impacts demand. When exploring where AI might fit into the potato system, we must first ask what constitutes a good outcome. A helpful framework for universally identified positive outcomes is the United Nations sustainable development goals, which include no poverty, zero hunger, and good health and well-being, among 17 goals. Narrowing down to potatoes, if we want more potatoes at a lower cost, we might introduce a mechanism to limit the impact of crop damage, creating more resilient capabilities and protecting crop yield. Ultimately, scoping the problem and using systems thinking allows us to understand the system, align successful outcomes with AI positioning, and anticipate potential inadvertent negative side effects or instability.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the most important and most difficult part of the AI project cycle?
Which of the following is given as an example of something that is complicated rather than complex?
In the predator-prey simulator and system diagrams, what are the connections between elements called?
What does a positive relationship mean in the context of system graphical views?
options: An increase in x leads to a decrease in y
An increase in x leads to an increase in y
A decrease in x leads to an increase in y
X and y remain completely independent
questions.correctAnswer: An increase in x leads to an increase in y

questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly listed as an element needed for growing potatoes in the French fry use case?
How many sustainable development goals are outlined by the United Nations as mentioned in the lesson?
What does a negative relationship represent in the system models?
options: An increase in x causes a decrease in y
An increase in x causes an increase in y
X and y have no relationship
Both x and y decrease simultaneously
questions.correctAnswer: An increase in x causes a decrease in y

questions.question: According to the simulator rules, what happens to the foxes if they go for a certain period of time without eating?
options: They migrate to a new ecosystem
